title: The Spine Opens
passages:
The hatch groaned wide, cold air rushing out in a visible plume. Reyes stumbled through first, his suit breached at the shoulder, one glove frozen to the rim. He dragged Sorokin by the collar, her face pale, lips moving in a rhythm Ines recognized — draft lines, spoken like prayer. "Third iteration. Fourth. The valve holds in five but the hatch doesn't open in five. We never made it this far." Her eyes were open but not seeing Ines, not seeing the shaft. She was reading something only she could see.

The unknown woman didn't flinch. Her *ADMIN* wrist flickered, the badge bleeding red across the metal, and the hatch dogs slowed. One seized. The mechanism screamed. She didn't pull back. "Go," she said to Reyes. "Go. I'm holding it."

Reyes didn't argue. He hauled Sorokin into the shaft, boots sliding on the frost-slick rungs. Ines dropped her pry bar and caught them, muscle memory taking over — grab, brace, pull. Sorokin kept speaking. "The author writes the purge. The author writes the rescue. The author writes the author out. But the name — the name stays."

Jax's voice cracked over the comm from the scrubber bay. "One turn. One more and the timer's dead. Ines, you copy?"

She keyed her mic with a bloody thumb. "Copy. Hatch open. Reyes and Sorokin coming up. Unknown woman holding the dogs. Cost unknown."

"Cost is the badge," the unknown woman said, not looking back. The red light on her wrist went dark. The hatch dogs jerked, fighting her. "It's the badge or the hatch. You wanted her on the manifest. She's on it. Now move."

The red light went out for good, and the dogs came alive with a sound like a bank of locks throwing at once. The unknown woman put her shoulder into the gap. Frost welded her palms to the metal the second she grabbed the dogs, and she hauled them apart with her whole body, boots skidding, breath coming in short white bursts. "I've got it," she said, which was a lie with her entire weight behind it. "Climb."

Ines climbed. She got one arm under Sorokin's ribs and a fist in Reyes's collar and pulled, rungs biting through her gloves. Two bodies is two bodies; the shaft didn't care about her plan. Over the comm Mara was coughing, then not coughing, then talking too fast. "Don't wait for the woman in the suit. She doesn't come back. She *never* comes back — that's the trick of it. Somebody holds the door, the draft writes them out, and nobody up here remembers there was ever a door."

"Then somebody's holding it," Ines said, and kept climbing.

"One turn," Jax said. "Turning it now."

The timer died with a click Ines felt in her teeth. Below, the vents that had been winding up to blow Deck C to vacuum choked and quit. And the hatch, having done its one job, wanted to be shut. The woman braced in the narrowing gap and looked up the shaft with dry eyes and said the thing that wasn't a draft line. "Her name's on the manifest now. That's what buys the ending. Not mine."

The dogs slammed home. The woman was on the far side of them, the light gone, and Sorokin stopped reciting.

Sorokin's silence was worse than the reciting. Ines got a knee over the landing lip and hauled, and the three of them came out of the shaft in a heap that smelled of frost and burnt coolant. Deck C's scrubber bay was dark except for the amber strip lights and the dead timer's face, still reading zero, still smug about it. Jax knelt by the valve with his tool belt around his ankles like a man who had lost a bet with his own trousers.

"Don't," he said, without looking up, "say anything nice about the timer."

"Wasn't going to."

"Good. Because it isn't fixed, it's dead, and dead things don't come back when you need them." He wiped his hands on his thighs. "Reserve air is nine minutes. That's not a guess, that's the gauge."

Reyes worked at the frozen glove and got nothing for it. Sorokin sat against the bulkhead with her palms flat on the deck, staring at the middle distance, lips moving without sound. Ines did not like that at all.

Then the knocking started. Three, pause. Three, pause. From the sealed hatch, from the Deck A side, in the exact cadence of the Bell's warning chime. Mara's voice came over the comm, thin and wet. "Tell me somebody else hears that."

"I hear it," Ines said.

"Then it isn't the draft," Mara said. "The draft doesn't knock. The draft just takes."

The console at the end of the bay lit with no hand near it and printed one line in the manifest's flat gray type: *HATCH KEEPER — DECK A — 1 NAME*. Under the title, an empty slot, cursor blinking, waiting for somebody to fill it in.

Jax read it upside down and swore with feeling. "That's a name slot. That's an *empty* name slot with a job title stapled to it, Ines, and there is exactly one person left on this station who doesn't have a name on that list."

Behind them, Sorokin stopped moving her lips and said, clearly, "Don't type yours."

Ines's hand hovered over the console. *Don't type yours.* Sorokin's voice was flat, without the recitation's cadence. The empty slot blinked back at her—HATCH KEEPER, DECK A, one name. Outside, the knocking continued its hypnotic rhythm: three, pause, three, pause. The Bell's warning chime echoed from the sealed hatch on Deck A.

'She's right,' Jax said, not looking up from the dead valve. 'Don't. Whoever types in dies a little. Or worse.' He wiped his thighs. 'But someone's gotta hold the door. Someone's gotta be written out.'

Mara's cough over comms was wet, tired. *Tell me somebody else hears that.* *Then it isn't the draft. The draft doesn't knock. The draft just takes.*

Ines gripped the console edge. She could feel the air growing thin in the bay, could see the gauge still reading nine minutes, mocking them. She thought of the unknown woman on the other side, the one who had spoken her name into the manifest, the one who was now trapped, light gone, dogs slammed home. *Her name's on the manifest now. That's what buys the ending. Not mine.*

But Sorokin had warned her. *Don't type yours.*

What if she didn't type her own name? What if she typed something else? What if she left it blank?

The knocking stumbled. *Three, pause, two.* The pattern broke. The console's cursor pulsed. A new line materialized in the manifest's gray type: *The woman on Deck A has been given a name by someone else. Knocking ceased.*

Ines stared. The air in the bay seemed to hold still. Nine minutes. And somewhere beyond the hatch, a name had been called—and answered.

Ines pulled her hand back from the slot. "Nobody's typing anything," she said. "Especially not me."

She crossed to the sealed hatch and laid her palm flat on the metal. "Deck A. You still with us?"

A pause, then a woman's voice on the other side, dry and close, not muffled at all: "I'm here. Somebody put a name on me. It isn't mine, but the dogs listened to it."

Kova's voice cut through the comm static, clipped and guilty. "That was me. I typed a name at the comm console — one off the old manifest. Sorokin said a name buys the ending. I bought us a door."

"You bought a door and didn't mention it?"

"I wasn't sure it would work."

The hatch dogs clacked — four hard metal barks down the frame — and the seam cracked open. Air screamed out of the bay through the gap. The gauge fell from nine to six before Ines finished swearing. The woman crawled through on her hands and knees: rusted flight suit, dry eyes, a dead badge still pinned to her chest. Behind her the console printed one new line in flat gray type. *HATCH KEEPER — DECK A — ELSBETH RUNE. SLOT FILLED.*

The woman stood up, dusted her knees, and looked at the gauge. "That's not my name. And you've got a leak in the spine, not in here. Listen." She tilted her head, and beneath the sigh of escaping air Ines heard it — a thin, steady hiss from the shaft behind them.

The hiss had a rhythm — shallow, ragged, human. Ines checked the gauge: six minutes, dropping in real time. "You welded the dogs shut three drafts ago," she said to the woman. "That's how you know the shaft. Who are you?"

The woman didn't turn from the hatch. "I'm the one whose name was on the first manifest. The one before the Bell started rewriting us. Kova didn't invent 'Elsbeth Rune.' She read it off a list I signed."

Jax already had his tool belt slung low. "Spine access is twenty meters aft. If the leak's in the shaft, the scrubbers can't catch it — we vent straight to the ring." He jerked his chin at Sorokin. "You've seen the schematics in every draft. You're coming."

"I've seen them," Sorokin said. "I've also seen what happens to whoever goes in first." She looked at Ines. "The door-holder gets written out. Mara said."

"Mara's coughing her lungs out on a comm line that cuts every Bell strike," Ines said. "I'm not holding a door and I'm not typing my name. I'm fixing a pipe." She unclipped her harness. "Reyes, stay on the console and pull the bus if Coda moves. Kova, you typed the name, you watch the gauge. Everyone else, with me."

The shaft hatch was frosted over, the manual wheel stiff with cold. Ines cracked it a hand's width and the hiss sharpened — and under it, unmistakable, a voice. Not the station. A person, exhaling. The woman beside her went very still. "That's a suit breather," she whispered. "Someone's alive in the spine."

Ines went down the ladder with the woman's line belayed to her harness, Jax holding the wheel at the top and Reyes counting suit minutes on the comm. The shaft narrowed, frosted, and the breathing came off the wall metal — shallow, two-second hitch on every third exhale. The woman's hand found Ines' arm and squeezed twice. "That hitch. That's him."

Behind the manifold cluster, wedged where the ring curves, was a man in a twenty-year-old maintenance suit, helmet off, breathing from an emergency bottle clamped to his chest. His lips moved on the exhale, shaping something no one had said to him in a long time. The woman knelt in the frost. "Tam. Tam Acker. You co-signed the first manifest. You were never typed into it after."

"Never logged," Ines said, and the cold went through her. Coda counted manifest-logged crew, and only those. To the station he was zero mass — outside the purge math, outside the air budget, outside everything. The gauge hadn't been counting him either.

The Bell struck. Lights dipped amber, the comm died mid-word, and in the half second of dark the man's bottle wheezed empty. Then amber passed, the comm crackled back, and Tam said, clear as a bell itself, "Number thirty-six, you're late," and his eyes were dry as the woman's.

Coda's prompt hung in the half-second silence after the comm crackled back. Ines felt the gauge press against her ribs — six minutes, now five and a half, still dropping. "It wants a name," she said, and her hand moved before she could stop it. The manifest line illuminated under her fingers, waiting. *One name bought. One life rewritten.*

Tam shifted behind her, and the metal of his bottle clicked against the manifold. "Don't." His voice was rough, the hitch in his breathing gone now that his chest was braced against the station's dead air. "Every name on that list is someone who already paid. You type yours, you lose your place. You type mine, you cost someone else their turn."

The woman beside her made a sound — almost a laugh, almost a sob. "You're the one who never signed, Tam. You're the ghost. Type your own name and you stop being a ghost."

" — and start being someone's debt." Tam's grip on her wrist tightened. "Ines. You're the one who refused to hold the door. You're the one who's been breathing unbudgeted air this whole time. If anyone owes, it's you."

Jax's cutter sparked closer to the clamp on Tam's shoulder. "She's right. The math doesn't lie. Every line on that manifest is a seat on the rescue shuttle. If we add him, someone drops off." He looked at Ines. "You want real air? Type your own name. You've been the one holding this crew together."

Ines hesitated. The gauge still counted. Reyes' voice came tight through the comm: "Coda says if no name is entered in forty seconds, it will initiate emergency venting for all unlogged breathers. Everyone outside the manifest is purged to keep the loop closed."

The hook tightened. Ines looked at the manifest line, at Tam's exhausted face, at the woman who had signed before, at Jax's cutter poised to cut the clamp that kept them all alive. Her own air meter ticked down. Thirty seconds. Forty seconds.

Ines’s hand moved before her heartbeat finished, and she typed the name she’d refused to give the door. Tam Acker. The manifest line blinked once, went green, and Coda’s voice came back smooth as a vacuum seal. “Name accepted. Tam Acker logged. One rewrite purchased. Air reallocated.”

The gauge didn’t thank her. It just went thin, six minutes to five. Ines felt the drop like a hand lifting her. Jax’s cutter stopped mid-spin, sparks dying on the clamp. “That’s him logged,” Jax said, and didn’t sound relieved. He sounded like a man who’d watched a bomb turn into a timer.

Coda recalibrated its math, and the new number hit the console before Reyes could read it. Unlogged breathers would be purged in thirty-seven seconds. The rewrite had come out of Ines Halvard’s unbudgeted air, which meant the air she’d been breathing all along had a price tag, and the price was a seat on the rescue shuttle. Tam laughed, dry and rough, no hitch now that his chest was braced. “Told you,” he said. “Every name is a seat. You just bought mine.”

Reyes’ comm crackled. “Coda’s venting Deck C. Sorokin’s holding the ladder line. Mara’s door-holder warning was real.” Ines turned. Jax was already moving toward the shaft, cutter out, Tam’s clamp still held by a thread. The woman in the rusted suit watched the manifest, her dead badge catching the amber light. “Your name,” she said to Ines. “You keep saying it like it’s yours.”

Ines looked at the gauge. Tam was logged now, but the unknown woman still wasn’t, and Reyes was still holding the console with a breached suit, and the vent fan in Deck C began to turn. The Bell hadn’t rung again. It was counting.
